newsitem.title: USA: Fed revises down U.S. industrial production.
newsitem.headline: Fed revises down U.S. industrial production.

text.p: The nation's industrial output grew a little more slowly than previously thought over the past 20 years, the Federal Reserve said Monday, and inflation pressures were slightly more muted.

The conclusion came from revised figures the central bank issued on production by the nation's mines, factories and utilities over the past two decades, part of an overhaul of the method to be used to calculate output.
"From 1977 to 1996, the annual rate of growth of total industrial production averaged 2.3 percent, about a quarter percentage point less than previously shown," the Fed said.

The Fed said its intent was to "eliminate an overstatement of the growth of production and capacity in earlier figures and...provide more accurate estimates of developments in industrial production and capacity utilization."

For example, December's industrial output increase was revised down to a 0.7 percent rise from a previously reported 0.8 percent gain. December's capacity use rate was revised to 83.5 percent from 83.8 percent.
For all of 1996, industrial output rose 2.7 percent instead of 3.2 percent as previously reported, the Fed said.
The revised figures also suggested slightly more breathing-room on inflation, since they show industries were not running quite as close to their limits as previously thought.
Capacity use rates, watched closely as a gauge of inflation pressures, peaked at a revised 84.9 percent during December 1994 and January 1995 instead of at 85.1 percent in those months, the Fed said.

As a rule of thumb, economists consider that an operating rate of 85 percent or higher risks fuelling inflation because it means factories are so busy they will be forced to pay more for supplies and labour used in manufacturing.
"The revised estimates show that capacity utilization reached its most recent high at the beginning of 1995, and that pressures on industrial capacity have been lower since then," the Fed said.

The Fed said in December that it planned to revise the industrial output and capacity use and to change its method of calculating the figures, updating the weighting given to particular industries annually instead of every five years.
Falling prices for computers, and their rising importance as a key sector for growth in industrial output, were a major factor in the revisions.

"Because of the rapid fall in the relative price of computers and peripheral equipment, the periodic updating of weights is too infrequent to provide reliable estimates of current changes in output, capacity and capacity utilization," the Fed said in December when it gave notice of the revisions.

The Fed said that, despite the revisions to industrial output and capacity use, the "cyclical profile" of the figures remains unchanged. There have been steady rises in annual output since the last recession that lasted from July 1990 through March 1991.

Industrial output contracted by 0.2 percent in 1990 with the onset of recession at mid-year and shrank 2 percent in 1991 despite the resumption of growth in the overall economy during the second quarter that year.
Since the last recession, industrial output grew 3.2 percent in 1992, 3.4 percent in 1993, 5 percent in 1994, 3.3 percent in 1995 and 2.7 percent last year.
